 PORTLAND, Ore. (KATU) — Federal election monitors will be watching over Multnomah County's voting process on Election Day, Nov. 3.
 The Oregon Secretary of State’s Office said the Civil Rights Division of the U.S. Department of Justice told them on Thursday the agency would send monitors to the county.
 “Oregon’s elections are secure, accurate and fair, and we always welcome observers to watch our American election process unfold,” said Oregon Secretary of State Tobias Read.
 Read also made it clear these observers, including federal officials, must follow state rules.
 “It is not legal for these observers or anyone else to interfere with Oregon's elections, even the Department of Justice. We are prepared. We will follow the law and we will make sure the Department of Justice does the same,” Read said.
 READ ALSO | Three candidates make their case to lead Multnomah County 
 Rules for observers 
 Multnomah County and other counties allow observers but protect the process with rules that forbid observers from talking to election workers, interfering with conversations between election workers and voters, taking photos or videos of sensitive voter information or handling any ballots or official materials.
 In an interview with KATU, Multnomah County Elections Director Tim Scott said federal observers will be treated like anyone else who comes to watch the county’s work.
 “They will not have access to ballots. They will not have access to secure rooms,” Scott said.
 Observers must sign an agreement to follow the county’s rules. Those who do not follow them can be excluded from the building, he said.
 Read told KATU that Scott and his staff would enforce those rules. Asked who would remove an observer who interfered with workers and refused to leave, Read expressed confidence in the county’s preparations but did not explain the removal process.
 DOJ’s role and Wyoming concerns 
 Federal monitors have been deployed for decades to protect against racial discrimination or intimidation at the polls.
 The Justice Department says its monitoring program promotes transparency, ballot security and compliance with federal voting rights laws, including protections for voters with disabilities. The department has conducted monitoring under previous administrations as well.
 Read said the department had discussed voter accessibility as a reason for its planned visit to Multnomah County.
 There is still caution in states across the country after reports of what some called “irregular” and “a bit aggressive” behavior by two Justice Department election monitors during Wyoming’s Aug. 18 primary election, according to reporting by the Associated Press. 
 Wyoming’s Republican governor, Mark Gordon, requested an investigation into the observers’ conduct, including requests to examine voting machines. A Justice Department official told Reuters the questions concerned access for voters with disabilities. The department also says its monitors are trained not to interfere with elections.
 How the county checks ballots 
 Scott described several checks that happen before a vote is counted.
 Workers check the barcode on each returned ballot envelope to confirm it is valid for the election. They also compare the signature on the envelope with the voter’s registration signature.
 If a signature does not match, the ballot stays inside its envelope and the county contacts the voter to resolve the problem, Scott said.
 Groups of workers from different political parties also take part at several stages, helping ensure decisions about how or whether a ballot is counted involve multiple people.
 The county keeps ballots and their envelopes for two years, so records are available if questions arise later.
 What voters should know 
 Read urged voters to contact their county elections office if they have not received a ballot.
 Anyone who sees concerning activity should contact elections officials or law enforcement rather than intervene, he said.
 Scott encouraged voters to return ballots early, giving workers more time to check them and contact voters if there is a problem.
 The Oregon Secretary of State’s Office said it will keep coordinating closely with county elections officials to make sure Oregon’s vote-by-mail election remains free and fair.
 Multnomah County Elections Director Tim Scott issued the following statement about DOJ election observers in the county: 
 “We are aware that the U.S. Department of Justice plans to send election monitors to Multnomah County. We are committed to transparency, and we routinely host monitors and community members of all political affiliations and backgrounds, so they can watch the dedicated and tireless work of our Elections staff and volunteers. 
 All election monitors, whether from the federal government or not, must follow all local rules and procedures, including a commitment not to interfere with elections work. We expect that our federal partners will be following our observer procedures just as we would for any group or individual. 
 We welcome election observers and support transparency and a proud tradition of holding open, accessible, secure and reliable elections. We will continue to reinforce trust in a system that has proven itself time and time again.”
